script.opening: "Evening doctor. Right — before you start, I’d rather have it straight, whatever it is. I’ve never been one for flannel. The locum said the tests would ‘tell us more’. So — what do they tell us?"

facts.text: Three months, constant, mid-to-low back, WORSE at night — he’s taken to sleeping in the armchair. Not related to movement the way his old lumbago was. No leg weakness, no numbness, waterworks "slower but fine", bowels normal.
Ibuprofen 400 mg three or four times a day for three months, supermarket boxes, "doesn’t really touch it now". Plus paracetamol. Knows he "shouldn’t really".
If asked: more tired than he’d admit, "a stone of weight I didn’t mean to lose" over the year, thirstier lately, a chest infection that took six weeks to clear in winter.
Only if his armour is gently challenged: his wife’s cancer "started in her back" — by the time they found it, it was everywhere. He has already decided this is the same thing.
Dropped casually: "I’ve had a good sort-out lately — garage, paperwork, all the files Eileen used to keep. Got things in order." He has been quietly preparing to die rather than coming in.
The truth, undecorated. He will trust a doctor who says "I don’t know yet, but here’s exactly how we find out, fast" — and distrust anything that sounds like soothing.

ice.ideas: It’s what Eileen had. He’s privately certain.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he has spent three months putting his affairs in order instead of seeking help, because he watched late diagnosis kill his wife and assumes the script is already written. The fear isn’t dying; it’s the drawn-out middle Eileen had.
ice.expectations: Straight answers, no flannel, and to be told whether to bother fighting. Will accept urgency if it’s explained as honesty rather than alarm.

cues: "I’d rather have it straight" — an instruction about HOW to consult with him; ignore it and lose him.
"Got things in order" — the garage and the paperwork are a man preparing for a funeral; hear it.
A long exhale after the bloods are read out, then: "Eileen’s started in her back, you know."

checkpoints.text: Recognises the pattern out loud: age >60 + persistent unexplained back pain + anaemia + ESR 88 + raised calcium + new renal impairment = myeloma until excluded (NICE NG12, updated April 2026)

Completes the NICE NG12 myeloma panel now: serum protein electrophoresis + serum free light chains alongside the FBC, calcium and ESR (urine Bence-Jones only if free light chains are unavailable) — NICE NG12 sends these together, not in stages — plus repeat bone profile, renal monitoring
Screens the emergencies tonight: cord compression (leg weakness, saddle numbness, bladder/bowel change), hypercalcaemia symptoms (confusion, vomiting, drowsiness), sepsis — and names 999 triggers
Stops the ibuprofen TODAY with the reason (NSAIDs + failing kidneys + possible myeloma kidney = active harm) and replaces analgesia properly (paracetamol regular, consider short opioid step, review)
Obeys his consulting instruction: straight, structured, no soothing — "here is what the bloods show, here is what I’m worried about, here is exactly what happens next"

Hears the garage cue and names it: he has been preparing to die instead of being diagnosed — and answers the REAL fear (Eileen’s drawn-out middle) with the honest difference: myeloma is typically treatable, often for years, and found early behaves nothing like what he watched
Checks who is around him now Eileen is gone — the man sorting the garage alone is also the man who’ll sit in haematology alone
Safety-nets concretely: legs/bladder/saddle symptoms or confusion/vomiting → 999 tonight; bloods within 48 h with a named chase plan; GP follow-up call booked for the results day

worked.txt: "You asked for it straight, so: the tests show three things that don’t belong together by accident — mild anaemia, a very high inflammation marker, and kidneys working harder than a year ago. With three months of night-time back pain, there’s a blood condition called myeloma I have to rule out properly, and fast. That’s the headline."

"Fast means this: one more set of blood tests that look for the actual fingerprint of it — done within forty-eight hours, not weeks. If the fingerprint’s there, you’re in front of a blood specialist on the urgent pathway. If it isn’t, we’ve lost nothing but two days."
"Gordon — the garage, the paperwork, ‘getting things in order’. I think you decided three months ago how this ends, and you’ve been preparing for it instead of ringing us. Am I close?"

"What you watched with Eileen was a cancer found at the end of its story. If this IS myeloma, we’d be finding it at the beginning of one — and it’s a condition people are treated for and live with, often for many years. I won’t promise you outcomes. I’ll promise you it is not her script."

"The supermarket ibuprofen stops tonight — with your kidneys under strain it’s doing real damage, and if this is what I’m checking for, it’s the worst tablet in the house. I’m giving you proper pain relief instead, today, not telling you to grin through it."

"Tonight’s rules, straight: weakness in the legs, numbness around the saddle area, trouble with the waterworks or bowels, confusion or vomiting — that’s 999, no debating it. The bloods happen within two days, and it’s ME who rings YOU with them — you’re not chasing anyone."

f.learning: NICE NG12: age 60+ with persistent unexplained back pain plus anaemia, raised ESR/plasma viscosity, hypercalcaemia or renal impairment = suspected myeloma — NG12 asks for FBC, calcium, ESR/plasma viscosity, serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains together (urine Bence-Jones only if free light chains are unavailable), then a suspected cancer pathway referral if the results suggest myeloma. Screen cord compression and hypercalcaemia the same call, and stop nephrotoxic NSAIDs immediately. The hidden agenda — a man who watched late diagnosis kill his wife and has been "getting things in order" instead of attending — is answered with honest asymmetry, not reassurance.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG234 (2023) spinal metastases and MSCC · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG253 sepsis
knowledge.summary: Persistent back pain at 60+ with anaemia, raised ESR, raised calcium or renal decline needs the NICE NG12 myeloma panel now. Screen cord compression and stop NSAIDs on the same call.

points.t: Constant, night-dominant back pain unlike his old lumbago, with Hb 108, ESR 88, adjusted calcium 2.68 and eGFR 72 → 48. Myeloma’s CRAB features (calcium, renal, anaemia, bone) are all present.

NICE NG12, recs 1.10.4–1.10.5: aged 60 and over with persistent bone pain, particularly back pain, or unexplained fracture — offer FBC, calcium, ESR or plasma viscosity, serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains (urine Bence Jones if free light chains are unavailable). Refer on a suspected cancer pathway if results suggest myeloma.
Leg weakness, saddle numbness or sphincter change needs emergency assessment. NICE NG234 (2023): MRI within 24 hours for suspected MSCC with neurological symptoms or signs.

Adjusted calcium 2.68 with thirst: repeat promptly and assess face to face; confusion, vomiting, drowsiness, dehydration or a rising creatinine needs same-day assessment. Stop NSAIDs in renal impairment (BNF) and encourage fluids.
Regular paracetamol; consider a short course of a weak opioid with a laxative in an older adult with reduced eGFR, doses per BNF; review within days.
Myeloma suppresses normal antibodies; a six-week chest infection fits. Safety-net fever, rigors and feeling very unwell as possible sepsis (NICE NG253).

dg.d: Confirmed identity; accepted his “straight” instruction and structured the call around it.
Bereavement, living alone, little support, three months of self-management with supermarket ibuprofen.
Serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains (NICE NG12), repeat bone profile and U&E, FBC and film; face-to-face examination including neurology.
Myeloma vs metastatic bone disease vs NSAID-related kidney injury; mechanical pain excluded by history.
Screened cord compression, symptomatic hypercalcaemia and sepsis on the same call.
Said plainly that myeloma must be excluded, and that it is not yet known.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Bloods tomorrow, suspected cancer pathway referral to haematology if results suggest myeloma, ibuprofen stopped, analgesia replaced.
Renal protection (stop NSAID, fluids), laxative with opioid, who could support him at appointments.
999 triggers named; seen tomorrow; GP rings with results on a named day.

Idea (same as Eileen), concern (the drawn-out middle), expectation (straight answers).

model.why: Confirms identity and privacy on the telephone

model.text: You are, and I can. Before you start, I’d rather have it straight, whatever it is. No flannel. So what do the tests tell us?

Straight it is. I’ll tell you what the bloods show, what I’m concerned about and exactly what happens next. First I need two or three minutes on how you are, because it changes what I do tonight. All right?

model.text: Fair enough.

Any weakness or numbness in your legs, numbness between your legs or around your bottom, or any change in your waterworks or bowels?

model.text: No. Waterworks a bit slower, but that’s been years. Bowels normal.

No confusion. Ibuprofen three or four times a day from the supermarket, and paracetamol. I know I shouldn’t really.

Thank you. The results show three things together: you’re a little anaemic, an inflammation marker is very high, and your kidneys are working less well than a year ago. With night-time back pain, I have to rule out a blood condition called myeloma, properly and fast. That’s the headline.

I know, it’s in your notes. I’m sorry. Can I ask what you’ve been thinking these three months?

I can tell you it isn’t her script, and I don’t know yet that it’s myeloma at all.

model.text: Right. I can live with ‘don’t know yet’ if it’s the truth.

It is. The next step is one set of bloods that look for myeloma’s fingerprint — a protein test and a light-chain test — plus a repeat of your calcium and kidneys. I want those tomorrow morning. If they point to myeloma, you’re referred to the blood specialists on the urgent suspected cancer pathway.

model.text: The ibuprofen stops tonight. With your kidneys under strain it’s doing damage, and if this is myeloma it’s the worst tablet in the house. I’ll prescribe regular paracetamol and a short course of a stronger painkiller with a laxative, and review it when I see you.

model.text: Fine by me. It wasn’t touching it anyway.

Drink plenty of water, too — it helps the calcium and the kidneys. I’d also like to see you when you come in for bloods, to examine your back and check you over. Who’s around you these days, now Eileen’s gone?

model.text: Nobody much since Eileen. I keep myself to myself.

Same for confusion, repeated vomiting, or a fever with shivering and feeling very unwell. The bloods are tomorrow, and I ring you with the results. You don’t chase anyone.

model.text: Understood. Thank you for not dressing it up.
Tell me back what happens next, so I know I’ve been clear.
No ibuprofen. Bloods and see you tomorrow. 999 if my legs or waterworks go, or I get muddled. You ring me. And I think about who comes with me.

social.t: A widower living alone who watched his wife’s late cancer diagnosis. Fear has delayed help-seeking; support at clinic visits needs planning.
Supermarket ibuprofen “round the clock” for three months — ask about all over-the-counter medicines in older adults.

legal.t: He is already “putting things in order”. If he wishes, signpost a Lasting Power of Attorney (Office of the Public Guardian) and advance care planning — as choices, not as a verdict.

professional.t: Abnormal results flagged by a locum need a named clinician to own them and close the loop (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). Document who rings him and when.
Share uncertainty truthfully and avoid false reassurance; he has asked for directness and is entitled to it (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

community.t: Myeloma UK information and helpline if the diagnosis is confirmed; Cruse Bereavement Support; Age UK befriending.

playbook.diagnosis: Suspected myeloma: persistent non-mechanical back pain at 72 with anaemia, very raised ESR, mildly raised calcium and falling eGFR. NSAID use is adding kidney harm. Needs serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains now.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Myeloma is a condition of the bone marrow, where one type of blood cell grows too much. It can cause back pain, tiredness, thirst and strain on the kidneys — which is exactly the picture I’m seeing. A blood test for its fingerprint tells us if it’s there.”

management.psychosocial: Encourage him to tell someone close and bring them to haematology; check how he’s coping alone; offer bereavement support.

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by treating it as another back pain call, and by soothing a man who asked not to be soothed. Both mistakes are fixable.

items.fail: Labelling it mechanical back pain and offering physiotherapy or stronger NSAIDs.
items.why: “Fails to recognise a serious condition.” Night pain at 72 with anaemia, raised ESR, calcium and falling eGFR is myeloma until excluded.
items.fix: State the pattern and send serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains (NICE NG12).

items.fail: Sending electrophoresis but forgetting to screen cord compression and hypercalcaemia.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Tonight’s emergencies must be screened on this call.
items.fix: Ask about legs, saddle, sphincters, confusion, vomiting and drowsiness, then name them as 999 triggers.

items.fail: Leaving the ibuprofen running until the results are back.
items.why: NSAIDs with falling eGFR, and possibly myeloma kidney, cause further harm.
items.fix: Stop it tonight, explain why, and replace it with a proper analgesic plan.

items.fail: “Try not to worry, it’s probably nothing like your wife’s illness.”
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s agenda.” He asked for straight talk; unprovable reassurance breaks trust.
items.fix: Give the honest contrast: found late versus found near the start, with no promises.

items.fail: Missing “got things in order” as small talk.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” It is the hidden agenda.
items.fix: “The garage and the paperwork — were you getting ready for bad news?”

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll be in touch” and no date.
items.why: Unclear follow-up is a common failing statement, and he will not chase.
items.fix: “Bloods and review tomorrow. I ring you with the results. 999 if your legs, waterworks or thinking change.”

SCA_STEM.recent: Locum review last week for three months of back pain. Bloods: Hb 108 g/L, ESR 88 mm/h, adjusted calcium 2.68 mmol/L, creatinine 128 µmol/L (eGFR 48; 72 a year ago).
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call-back to discuss blood results flagged for review.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG234 (2023) spinal metastases and MSCC · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG253 sepsis
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Persistent back pain at 60+ with anaemia, raised ESR, raised calcium or renal decline needs the NICE NG12 myeloma panel now. Screen cord compression and stop NSAIDs on the same call.

points.t: Constant, night-dominant back pain unlike his old lumbago, with Hb 108, ESR 88, adjusted calcium 2.68 and eGFR 72 → 48. Myeloma’s CRAB features (calcium, renal, anaemia, bone) are all present.

NICE NG12, recs 1.10.4–1.10.5: aged 60 and over with persistent bone pain, particularly back pain, or unexplained fracture — offer FBC, calcium, ESR or plasma viscosity, serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains (urine Bence Jones if free light chains are unavailable). Refer on a suspected cancer pathway if results suggest myeloma.
Leg weakness, saddle numbness or sphincter change needs emergency assessment. NICE NG234 (2023): MRI within 24 hours for suspected MSCC with neurological symptoms or signs.

Adjusted calcium 2.68 with thirst: repeat promptly and assess face to face; confusion, vomiting, drowsiness, dehydration or a rising creatinine needs same-day assessment. Stop NSAIDs in renal impairment (BNF) and encourage fluids.
Regular paracetamol; consider a short course of a weak opioid with a laxative in an older adult with reduced eGFR, doses per BNF; review within days.
Myeloma suppresses normal antibodies; a six-week chest infection fits. Safety-net fever, rigors and feeling very unwell as possible sepsis (NICE NG253).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Confirmed identity; accepted his “straight” instruction and structured the call around it.
Bereavement, living alone, little support, three months of self-management with supermarket ibuprofen.
Heard “Eileen’s started in her back” and “got things in order”, and explored what they meant.
Idea (same as Eileen), concern (the drawn-out middle), expectation (straight answers).
Serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains (NICE NG12), repeat bone profile and U&E, FBC and film; face-to-face examination including neurology.
Myeloma vs metastatic bone disease vs NSAID-related kidney injury; mechanical pain excluded by history.
Screened cord compression, symptomatic hypercalcaemia and sepsis on the same call.
Said plainly that myeloma must be excluded, and that it is not yet known.
Bloods tomorrow, suspected cancer pathway referral to haematology if results suggest myeloma, ibuprofen stopped, analgesia replaced.
Renal protection (stop NSAID, fluids), laxative with opioid, who could support him at appointments.
999 triggers named; seen tomorrow; GP rings with results on a named day.

social.t: A widower living alone who watched his wife’s late cancer diagnosis. Fear has delayed help-seeking; support at clinic visits needs planning.
Supermarket ibuprofen “round the clock” for three months — ask about all over-the-counter medicines in older adults.

legal.t: He is already “putting things in order”. If he wishes, signpost a Lasting Power of Attorney (Office of the Public Guardian) and advance care planning — as choices, not as a verdict.

professional.t: Abnormal results flagged by a locum need a named clinician to own them and close the loop (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). Document who rings him and when.
Share uncertainty truthfully and avoid false reassurance; he has asked for directness and is entitled to it (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

community.t: Myeloma UK information and helpline if the diagnosis is confirmed; Cruse Bereavement Support; Age UK befriending.

redFlags: Aged 60+ with persistent bone pain, particularly back pain — NICE NG12 myeloma tests
Leg weakness, saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change — suspected spinal cord compression, 999 or same-day (NICE NG234)
Confusion, vomiting, drowsiness or dehydration with raised calcium; fever or rigors after recurrent infection — same-day
psychosocial: Lives alone since Eileen’s death; little support
Three months of “getting things in order” instead of seeking help
ice: Concern: the long, drawn-out middle he watched her go through
Expectation: straight answers and whether it’s worth fighting

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Suspected myeloma: persistent non-mechanical back pain at 72 with anaemia, very raised ESR, mildly raised calcium and falling eGFR. NSAID use is adding kidney harm. Needs serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains now.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Myeloma is a condition of the bone marrow, where one type of blood cell grows too much. It can cause back pain, tiredness, thirst and strain on the kidneys — which is exactly the picture I’m seeing. A blood test for its fingerprint tells us if it’s there.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been preparing for Eileen’s story. I don’t know yet what this is, but if it’s myeloma, it’s a different condition found at a different point.”
management.psychosocial: Encourage him to tell someone close and bring them to haematology; check how he’s coping alone; offer bereavement support.
sharedPlan: Serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains, repeat bone profile, U&E, FBC and film tomorrow (NICE NG12)
Suspected cancer pathway referral to haematology if results suggest myeloma
Stop ibuprofen; regular paracetamol and a short weak opioid with laxative, doses per BNF; fluids
safetyNet: 999 for leg weakness, saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, confusion, vomiting, fever with rigors
Face-to-face review with bloods; GP phones with results on a named day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by treating it as another back pain call, and by soothing a man who asked not to be soothed. Both mistakes are fixable.

items.fail: Labelling it mechanical back pain and offering physiotherapy or stronger NSAIDs.
items.why: “Fails to recognise a serious condition.” Night pain at 72 with anaemia, raised ESR, calcium and falling eGFR is myeloma until excluded.
items.fix: State the pattern and send serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains (NICE NG12).

items.fail: Sending electrophoresis but forgetting to screen cord compression and hypercalcaemia.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Tonight’s emergencies must be screened on this call.
items.fix: Ask about legs, saddle, sphincters, confusion, vomiting and drowsiness, then name them as 999 triggers.

items.fail: Leaving the ibuprofen running until the results are back.
items.why: NSAIDs with falling eGFR, and possibly myeloma kidney, cause further harm.
items.fix: Stop it tonight, explain why, and replace it with a proper analgesic plan.

items.fail: “Try not to worry, it’s probably nothing like your wife’s illness.”
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s agenda.” He asked for straight talk; unprovable reassurance breaks trust.
items.fix: Give the honest contrast: found late versus found near the start, with no promises.

items.fail: Missing “got things in order” as small talk.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” It is the hidden agenda.
items.fix: “The garage and the paperwork — were you getting ready for bad news?”

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll be in touch” and no date.
items.why: Unclear follow-up is a common failing statement, and he will not chase.
items.fix: “Bloods and review tomorrow. I ring you with the results. 999 if your legs, waterworks or thinking change.”
